metadata.note: Rochester's city streetcar network at its through-routed peak - 19 routes, about 240 km of track as traced here. Street railways in Rochester began with the Rochester City & Brighton Rail Road, incorporated May 31, 1862, whose first horsecar line ran from the company's State Street headquarters to Mount Hope and opened in July 1863; by October 1863 it had 6.6 miles of track, 18 cars and 48 horses working Main Street, Buffalo Street to West Avenue, and Alexander Street to Monroe Avenue. A group of Pittsburgh investors bought it in 1890 as the Rochester Railway Company, leased the Rochester Electric Railway in 1894, and had all lines electrified by 1894; the Rochester & Suburban was leased in 1905, reaching Irondequoit and Sea Breeze. The company passed to the Mohawk Valley Company, a New York Central subsidiary assembling electric railways in its territory, and was consolidated into the New York State Railways in 1909 as its Rochester Lines. Until 1912 most lines simply began and ended downtown on Main Street; after that they were paired into continuous through routes crossing the city - which is why almost every route on this map carries two street names, a west or north side street joined to an east or south side one. New York State Railways went into receivership in 1929 and the Rochester Transit Corporation took over the Rochester Lines on August 2, 1938, having already won Public Service Commission approval to substitute buses. The conversion ran from March 28, 1939 (Genesee Street) to March 31, 1941, when the Main East and Lake Avenue lines closed together; the last streetcar ran in the city on April 1, 1941. Streetcar operation survived only in the Rochester Subway, which lasted until 1956 and is mapped separately as rochester_subway.geojson.

geometry_sources: Traced along MODERN STREET GEOMETRY from OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API), not from abandoned-railway tagging - Rochester's streetcars ran in the public streets, so almost none of the network survives as mapped rail. About 11,200 named road ways were pulled for the Rochester area and built into a routing graph of 87,453 nodes. Each route was then routed by Dijkstra with a name-aware cost: travel along the streets the route is NAMED for costs its true length, travel along recognised downtown connector streets (Main, State, Exchange, Clinton, Plymouth, Court, Broad and similar) costs 3x, and travel along any other street costs 30x. The result follows the actual named streets and only leaves them where it must to connect. Every metre of all 19 routes is real street geometry - there is NO straight-line approximation anywhere in this file.

Outer termini were chosen from the data rather than by hand: for each route the algorithm takes the farthest point of its named street from the Four Corners (Main at State/Exchange, 43.1566,-77.6115) within the Rochester city box, with a tighter bounding box supplied where a street name recurs elsewhere in the county (there is a second Park Avenue in Gates, a second Jefferson Avenue and several East Avenues).

Every route name in the sourced roster was checked against OSM and found to be a real Rochester street lying where expected - Lake, Park, Thurston, Parsells, Lyell, Bay, Genesee, University, Saint Paul, South, Jefferson, Webster, Monroe, North Clinton, East Main, Chili, Hudson, Mount Read, Dewey, Portland, Joseph, South Clinton, North/South Goodman, West, Culver, West/East Ridge, Norton, Britton, Emerson, East, South Plymouth, Clifford and Titus. That is the check that grounds the network: the route names ARE street names.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: IMPORTANT - the STREET IDENTITY of each route is sourced (the roster names the streets), but the exact ROUTING is reconstructed, not taken from a historical route map. Specifically: outer termini are the ends of each named street rather than sourced car-line terminals, so a route may be drawn slightly longer or shorter than it really ran; the downtown linking between each pair of streets is the router's shortest sensible path along Main Street and its connectors, not a documented alignment; and the through-route pairings are taken from the roster's names (Lake/Park and so on) without a source for where each pair actually met. The Goodman/West and Norton/Britton pairings are the least certain - both join streets that do not obviously connect, and their downtown or cross-city links here are the router's inference. No frequencies are sourced; every headway below is estimated. Closure years are sourced for eight routes (see each feature's final segment); the other eleven are given 1941 because the whole system was converted to buses by then, not because a date is recorded for them. Finally, the 1863-1889 HORSECAR network is deliberately NOT drawn: it totalled only 6.6 miles in 1863 against roughly 240 km here, and drawing the modern full-length routes back to 1863 would badly misrepresent it - so every feature starts in 1890, the year the Rochester Railway Company took over and began electrification.
metadata.horsecar_audit: 2026-08-24: adjusted in a repo-wide horsecar audit. The first segment of all 19 features began in 1890, when the Rochester Railway Company bought a system that was still partly horse-drawn and did not finish electrifying until 1894; all have been moved to start in 1894. Electrification was progressive over those four years, so some individual lines went electric earlier and are now drawn slightly short -- 1894 is the conservative choice, since it is the year animal haulage is documented to have ended system-wide. REPO RULE 5: this map shows MECHANICALLY powered rail -- horsecars and mule cars are out of scope, and a line's drawn years must start when it stopped using animals. Notes may still mention the animal era as context. See CLAUDE.md.
metadata.color_unification: 2026-08-24: collapsed to one colour per CLAUDE.md Rule 4, which allows no exception for transit agencies that brand each line differently. All 19 routes belong to one company string and now share #C1272D. Rule 4's usual tie-break -- the most-used existing hex -- had no answer here because each of the 19 routes carried a distinct colour used exactly once, so the colour was taken from the longest route (roc-streetcar-norton-britton, 23.9 km). Each feature keeps its original per-route hex in a 'former_route_color' property, which app.js ignores, so the old scheme is recoverable. This matches how the peer file syracuse_streetcars.geojson already handles its city network with a single colour.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
